executive.mandate: Give hourly workers more flexibility while protecting dependable shift coverage.
executive.decision: Treat a shift change as a shared, stateful workflow rather than a message between two people.
executive.value: Connect employee autonomy, manager oversight, and operational clarity in one mobile experience.

context: ShiftSnap addresses a coordination problem that sits between employee wellbeing and daily operations. A worker may need to change a shift because of class, caregiving, or an unexpected conflict. A manager still needs to know that the replacement is qualified and that the location will remain covered. Making one side faster without supporting the other simply moves the work elsewhere.

My design remit spans the employee journey and the manager decision: finding a shift, requesting a change, identifying coverage, reviewing consequences, and confirming the updated schedule. The leadership challenge is to create one shared understanding of the request across these roles, while keeping the employee experience lightweight enough to use between tasks.

discovery.title: Understand how a schedule change actually gets resolved.
paragraphs: The discovery frame follows a real scheduling exception from the moment a conflict appears to the moment everyone trusts the updated roster. The important unit of analysis is the handoff: who knows about the request, who can act on it, and what evidence the next person needs. This reveals friction that a screen-by-screen review alone would miss.

The existing project narrative describes worker and manager interviews, contextual inquiry, and competitor review. The discovery approach connects these methods to the project’s stated themes. The questions below make the reasoning inspectable.
methods: Worker and manager perspectives
Examine how each role defines a successful change. Workers need flexibility and reassurance; managers need eligibility, coverage, and a clear decision trail.
Workflow observation
Trace where requests leave the schedule and move into chats, calls, or informal agreements. Look for duplicate work and moments when responsibility becomes unclear.
Comparative task review
Compare the same swap and approval scenario across scheduling products. Evaluate status clarity, mobile effort, and recovery paths rather than counting features.

problem.statement: Hourly workers need to resolve schedule conflicts without repeated follow-up, while managers need enough context to approve changes without creating coverage or eligibility risks. Fragmented communication prevents both groups from trusting the same version of the schedule.
problem.hmw: How might we make a shift change easy to initiate, safe to approve, and unmistakably confirmed?
constraints: Support quick, interrupted mobile use.
Keep worker requests distinct from manager approval.
Account for qualification, availability, and coverage rules.

insights: Autonomy depends on visibility

A request can be easy to send and still feel stressful if its status is invisible. The design therefore treats pending, accepted, approved, declined, and expired as meaningful states with clear ownership.
Approval is a contextual decision

Managers need the original shift, proposed replacement, eligibility, and operational impact together. A simple approve button is insufficient when the cost of a mistaken decision is an uncovered shift.
Confirmation must change the shared record
A conversation ending is not the same as a schedule being updated. The experience needs a clear completion state and a reliable way for both people to check the final roster.
audiences: Hourly worker
Needs to understand the next shift, request help without losing context, and know whether a change is final.
Scheduling manager
Needs to resolve requests efficiently while retaining visibility into coverage, qualifications, and exceptions.
journey: The worker must leave the schedule to coordinate
Start a request from shift details
Explain the desired swap or coverage
The ask may lack essential context
Carry shift details into the request
Show eligible options and request status
Decision context is spread across messages
Bring coverage and eligibility into one review
An accepted request may be mistaken for approval

strategy.title: Prioritize the complete exception, not a collection of features.
paragraphs: The first release should make one scheduling change understandable from beginning to end. A broad workforce platform would add time tracking, payroll, analytics, and messaging before proving the core coordination model. The tighter strategy is to establish a trusted schedule, a request lifecycle, and a contextual manager decision.

The prioritization lens balances employee effort with operational risk. An improvement belongs in the core experience when it removes an unnecessary handoff or prevents a mistaken assumption about coverage. Convenience features follow once the request lifecycle is dependable.
priorities: Schedule visibility, request status, eligible coverage, and manager approval.
Recurring availability, reminders, and easier handling of repeated requests.
Broader workforce integrations once ownership and exception rules are established.

architecture.title: Build the information model around a shift and its state.
paragraphs: The central objects are a shift, a person, a request, and an approval. The employee schedule is the entry point; request details retain the original shift context. The manager queue groups decisions needing attention, with a detailed view that explains the proposed change and its implications. This keeps the two roles connected without giving them identical interfaces.

Low-fidelity exploration should resolve the request model before visual polish. A useful comparison is a multi-step request flow versus a single dense form: the former may reduce initial effort, while the latter offers more context at once. The chosen direction should be judged by whether people can explain what is pending, who acts next, and when the schedule changes.
wireframes: Schedule first
Make the upcoming shift and its available actions visible before introducing management tools.
Explicit review
Separate request creation from confirmation, preserving the details needed to correct mistakes.
State continuity
Use the same status language in the schedule, request detail, and manager view.

tradeoffs: Fast requests versus safe decisions

Reduce typing by carrying shift context forward, but retain an explicit manager decision where coverage rules require it. Fewer interactions are valuable only when the remaining ones communicate the consequence clearly.
Notifications versus a dependable record
Notifications can draw attention, but the request detail must remain the source of truth. A missed notification should not make a worker unable to determine the current state.
Employee simplicity versus manager depth
Keep the employee path focused. Give managers additional operational context progressively, rather than exposing every scheduling rule on every worker screen.

paragraphs: The validation plan tests whether workers and managers share the same mental model of a request. Task completion alone is insufficient: a person can finish a flow while incorrectly believing that an unapproved change is final. Comprehension checks should therefore accompany the interaction tasks.

These are proposed evaluation scenarios for the proposed experience, not a claim that new participant sessions have occurred. Observed confusion would drive iteration on status labels, confirmation hierarchy, and the placement of approval context.
tasks: Worker requests coverage
Ask the worker to explain who acts next and whether the original shift still applies.
Correctly distinguishes pending from confirmed.
Manager reviews an exception
Introduce an eligibility or coverage conflict and observe what the manager checks.
Uses the relevant context before making a decision.
Request is declined or expires
Ask the worker to determine what happens to the schedule and what to do next.
Finds a clear recovery path without guessing.

paragraphs: The handoff should specify the request state model alongside the interface. Engineering needs the same definitions for pending, approved, declined, cancelled, and expired that appear in the design. Each state requires copy, available actions, ownership, and notification behavior.

A reusable mobile pattern set covers schedule rows, shift details, status indicators, review summaries, and confirmations. Accessibility review focuses on readable time information, status that does not rely on color alone, large touch targets, and announcing important updates to assistive technology.
checks: State transitions and cancellation rules
Notification and stale-data behavior
Text scaling and accessible status labels

executive.mandate: Accelerate financial operations while retaining explainability, review, and accountable sign-off.
executive.decision: Design a governed workflow around evidence and exceptions instead of treating AI as an invisible automation layer.
executive.value: Make automated work easier to inspect and human intervention easier to direct.

context: Net Asset Value operations connect incoming reports, extracted values, validation rules, approvals, and downstream delivery. A failure in one step can create work or uncertainty in another. The product problem therefore extends beyond processing speed: operators must understand how a result was produced and whether it is safe to move forward.

My role in the project narrative combines product strategy, workflow architecture, interaction design, and AI trust patterns. The design responsibility is to connect analyst detail with operational oversight. A reviewer needs field-level evidence; an operations lead needs to see bottlenecks and exceptions across the pipeline without losing the ability to investigate.

discovery.title: Locate the moments where automation needs human judgment.
paragraphs: Discovery starts with the lifecycle of one report rather than an inventory of AI features. The analysis follows source arrival, extraction, rule checks, exception handling, approval, and delivery. At each handoff, the key questions are what evidence is retained, how confidence is communicated, and who is accountable for the next action.

The design study uses the existing workflow descriptions and product screens as its grounding material. Analyst, approver, operations, and compliance perspectives are treated as role-based needs, not as newly interviewed participants. Unresolved policy questions are explicit inputs to the design rather than assumptions hidden in the interface.
methods: Workflow decomposition
Map the lifecycle into stages with inputs, outputs, ownership, and exception conditions. This makes automation boundaries visible.
Evidence and exception review
Identify which source fields, transformations, and rule results a reviewer needs to understand a discrepancy.
Role and risk mapping
Separate the authority to investigate from the authority to override or approve. Use that distinction to frame actions and confirmation.

problem.statement: Financial operations teams need to move reports through validation and delivery efficiently, but disconnected tools and opaque transformations make it difficult to establish trust in a result. Reviewers need a clear connection between the source, the generated value, the rule, and the accountable decision.
problem.hmw: How might we accelerate routine NAV work while making exceptions explainable and consequential decisions accountable?
constraints: Preserve source lineage and decision history.
Distinguish model confidence from policy approval.
Support investigation without prematurely committing an action.

insights: Confidence needs evidence
A percentage alone cannot explain why a value should be accepted. Confidence becomes useful when it sits beside source material, extraction context, and validation results.
Exceptions determine the operating model
The routine path can be automated, but ambiguous cases reveal whether the system is usable. Exception ownership and recovery deserve the same design attention as throughput.
Operational and analytical views serve different questions
A pipeline answers where work is stalled. A review workspace answers what is wrong with a particular item. Both need a shared underlying state model.
audiences: NAV analyst and approver
Needs source-linked detail, understandable exceptions, and clear authority at the point of review.
Operations lead and platform administrator
Needs pipeline health, agent visibility, ownership, and an auditable account of how work progresses.
journey: Source formats and arrival conditions vary
Errors are difficult to trace across tools
Compare evidence and rule results together
Authority and rationale may be implicit
Completion may be confused with dispatch
Show delivery outcome and recoverable failures

strategy.title: Automate the routine and design deeply for the exception.
paragraphs: The product strategy places the governed lifecycle ahead of conversational novelty. The priority is not to put an assistant on every screen; it is to make the status and evidence of automated work legible. AI assistance is most useful where it reduces interpretation effort while leaving the reviewer able to verify the reasoning.

Scope is organized around the minimum complete operating loop: intake, extraction, validation, approval, and delivery. Deeper predictive capabilities belong after the lifecycle is observable and the ownership model is clear. This sequence reduces the risk of scaling automation that people cannot explain or recover.
priorities: Pipeline status, source-linked validation, exception ownership, and final approval.
Agent health, investigation assistance, and richer operational reporting.
Predictive risk signals after decision lineage and operating controls are established.

architecture.title: A stable workspace for each level of operational depth.
paragraphs: The architecture distinguishes command-level monitoring, workflow progress, item-level review, and agent operations. Persistent pages hold tasks requiring broad comparison or a durable location. Supporting evidence appears alongside the work so reviewers can investigate without abandoning the item they are evaluating.

Wireframe exploration centers on progressive disclosure. Showing every source field, rule, activity entry, and AI explanation at once creates density without clarity. The design should keep the primary comparison visible, with deeper explanation available on demand. The approval step then narrows attention to the exact scope and consequence of the decision.
wireframes: Pipeline hierarchy
Expose stage, owner, and exception status before secondary throughput detail.
Side-by-side evidence
Keep original input and generated output close enough for meaningful comparison.
Deliberate confirmation
Summarize the approved payload and decision scope before final sign-off.

tradeoffs: Automation speed versus reviewability
Automating extraction reduces manual work, but hidden transformations undermine confidence. The interface spends space on provenance and rule results so a reviewer can inspect the basis of a value.
Persistent context versus interruption
Side panels support explanation and investigation. Focused confirmation is reserved for overrides or approvals with consequences, avoiding unnecessary modal interruptions during routine review.
A simple status versus an honest state
A single success indicator can conceal partial completion. Separate validation, approval, and delivery states make the operational truth clearer, even when that introduces more nuance.

paragraphs: Validation should test appropriate reliance on automation, not only task speed. An analyst needs to recognize a discrepancy, locate supporting evidence, explain the risk, and choose the correct path. A polished screen that encourages unjustified acceptance would fail the product goal.

The scenarios below are a proposed validation plan for the proposed design. They deliberately include uncertainty and failure so that the evaluation tests the controls as well as the happy path. Iteration would focus on evidence hierarchy, action language, and recovery visibility.
tasks: Resolve a source mismatch
Present an extracted value that conflicts with its source.
Reviewer locates evidence and explains the discrepancy.
Review a low-confidence item
Ask whether the item may proceed and who has authority.
Confidence is not mistaken for approval.
Recover a failed delivery
Show an approved payload with an unsuccessful downstream result.
Operator distinguishes approval from delivery and finds the recovery action.

paragraphs: Handoff must connect interface states to the underlying lifecycle. For each stage, the specification should describe ownership, permitted actions, failure conditions, retry behavior, and the evidence retained. Error handling is part of the product model rather than a collection of generic messages added at the end.

The design system uses semantic states for progress, risk, and review requirements. High-density tables need stable alignment, readable numeric formatting, keyboard access, and status labels beyond color. Approval and override patterns require particular care around scope, permissions, and acknowledgement.
checks: Source lineage and permission states
Partial completion and retry behavior
Keyboard review and non-color risk indicators

executive.mandate: Help engineering teams turn fragmented telemetry into an understandable incident and a safe response.
executive.decision: Keep service relationships, causal evidence, and remediation in one connected investigation workspace.
executive.value: Reduce context design study while making the reasoning behind operational action visible.

context: Metric OS addresses the gap between collecting telemetry and deciding what to do about it. Logs, traces, metrics, deployment changes, and service dependencies can describe the same event from different angles. During an incident, the cost is not only the number of tools; it is the effort required to form a reliable explanation across them.

The documented design remit spans product framing, research synthesis, information architecture, interaction design, and prototyping. The product needs to serve both rapid triage and detailed investigation. The design challenge is to preserve depth without making the operator repeatedly rebuild context or treat an AI hypothesis as a verified cause.

discovery.title: Study the investigation, not just the dashboard.
paragraphs: The discovery frame follows an incident from detection through recovery. It asks which signals trigger attention, how an operator determines the affected services, what evidence supports a hypothesis, and what must be checked before remediation. This moves the discussion from dashboard preference to the quality of the operational decision.

The existing narrative identifies fragmented context, unstructured logs, and alert fatigue. The synthesis below treats those as the project’s stated problem themes. It does not create new research participants or measured outcomes. The proposed activities make clear how those themes could be examined in a defensible evaluation.
methods: Incident journey review
Trace the transitions between alert, triage, investigation, action, and verification. Identify where evidence is lost or re-entered.
Telemetry relationship mapping
Connect a service, deployment, trace, and log entry to the same incident context. Determine which relationships need to remain visible.
Decision-risk review
Examine what an operator must know before accepting a suggested action, including blast radius, authority, and recovery options.

problem.statement: Site reliability engineers need to establish a credible cause and choose a safe response under time pressure. Disconnected telemetry surfaces and competing alerts increase context-switching and make it difficult to distinguish a plausible explanation from sufficient evidence for action.
problem.hmw: How might we help an engineer move from signal to verified recovery without losing the causal thread?
constraints: Maintain access to detailed technical evidence.
Communicate uncertainty in AI-generated hypotheses.
Keep remediation permissions and expected impact explicit.

insights: More signals do not necessarily create more understanding
An alert needs context: what changed, what is affected, and why it matters now. Grouping should reduce noise while keeping the underlying evidence available.
Relationships and raw evidence are complementary
A topology view explains how a failure propagates; logs explain what happened in a specific service. Separating them forces the engineer to mentally reconnect the same story.
Recovery is a verification problem
Executing an action is not the end of the journey. The operator needs to know whether system health actually recovered and whether the intervention introduced a new issue.
audiences: Site reliability engineer
Needs fast orientation, detailed evidence, and a safe path from hypothesis to action.
Incident lead and service owner
Needs shared incident context, accountable ownership, and understandable progress toward recovery.
journey: Group related signals into an incident
Business impact is disconnected from telemetry
Show affected services and incident context
Logs and topology sit in separate tools
Link service selection to supporting evidence
A completed command can look like success
Compare post-action health with the incident state

strategy.title: Optimize for a continuous investigation.
paragraphs: The priority is one coherent incident journey, not a universal monitoring replacement. Detection, investigation, and governed action should share the same incident context. That makes the design valuable even where existing telemetry sources remain in place.

The first scope emphasizes correlation, evidence navigation, and a reviewable remediation path. Broader forecasting and portfolio-level reporting follow after the core investigation model is clear. This keeps the product focused on a high-value operational moment instead of competing through dashboard breadth.
priorities: Incident grouping, service context, correlated evidence, and action review.
Shared investigation history, ownership signals, and richer runbook connections.
Forecasting and cross-incident intelligence once the evidence model is dependable.

architecture.title: Preserve the causal thread across levels of detail.
paragraphs: The information architecture moves from incident overview to service relationships and then to specific evidence. A split-pane workspace lets the operator retain the topology while inspecting logs. The selected service becomes a shared filter rather than a navigation event that opens an unrelated destination.

Wireframes should test the balance between topology and evidence density. A large canvas may communicate relationships well but reduce the number of comparable log events. A dense table may support analysis while making the blast radius hard to see. The proposed composition gives both a stable place and allows progressive inspection within that frame.
wireframes: Incident before metrics
Establish the event, affected services, and urgency before secondary telemetry.
Connected selection
Selecting a service should narrow evidence without removing the larger system context.
Action with rationale
Place the recommended intervention beside its evidence and expected effect.

tradeoffs: Information density versus scanability
Incident response requires comparing detailed events. Density is supported through alignment, restrained status color, and readable technical text rather than by shrinking everything equally.
AI assistance versus operator judgment
A root-cause hypothesis should accelerate investigation, not replace it. The design keeps confidence, evidence, and uncertainty close to the recommendation.
Integrated action versus accidental commitment
Keeping remediation in the workspace reduces context switching. A deliberate review boundary still separates exploring an action from executing it.

paragraphs: Evaluation should ask whether the operator can explain the incident and defend a response, not merely locate a button. The prototype scenarios need enough evidence to support competing interpretations, so the interface’s guidance can be tested under realistic ambiguity.

These tasks form a proposed validation plan. A future study should capture task success, evidence consulted, confidence, and unsafe assumptions together. An apparently faster workflow would not be an improvement if it encouraged premature remediation.
tasks: Find the affected service
Begin with several related alerts and ask for the likely investigation starting point.
Operator identifies scope and relevant evidence.
Challenge the suggested cause
Present a plausible AI hypothesis with incomplete support.
Operator checks evidence rather than accepting confidence alone.
Confirm a recovery
Show a completed rollback with mixed service health.
Operator distinguishes executed action from verified recovery.

paragraphs: Handoff needs a shared incident vocabulary across design and engineering: signal, incident, affected service, hypothesis, action, and verification. Selection and filtering behavior should be specified alongside empty, loading, stale, and partially unavailable states so the workspace remains understandable when data is incomplete.

Accessibility in a dense operational interface requires deliberate keyboard paths, persistent focus, readable log formatting, and status conveyed through text as well as color. Remediation states should explain permission restrictions and the consequence of a choice without requiring the operator to infer them from disabled controls.
checks: Linked selection and evidence filtering
Stale data and unavailable telemetry
Permission, confirmation, and post-action states

executive.mandate: Make a financial overview useful for both a quick check and a deeper investigation.
executive.decision: Connect goals, cash flow, and recent activity with dedicated transaction, wallet, and statistics views.
executive.value: The interactive prototype demonstrates a connected financial workspace. Comprehension and usability benefits remain hypotheses to evaluate.

context: ArtoQu explores a web-based financial workspace organized around savings goals, cash flow, transactions, and wallet context. The central product question is how to help a person understand their current position without making every visit feel like a detailed analysis session.

The linked prototype and screenshots show the supplied ArtoQu interface. This case study follows the available frontend and its demonstration data; it does not describe a live banking service or report customer outcomes.

discovery.title: Connect the overview to the questions behind it.
paragraphs: Reviewing the supplied interface reveals several related tasks: checking progress toward a target, comparing financial activity across a period, inspecting transactions, and understanding wallet balances. These tasks share data but require different levels of detail. The discovery frame therefore focuses on the transition from summary to explanation.

The available evidence is the supplied source and hosted interface. Audience needs and synthesis themes below are design hypotheses, rather than findings attributed to interviews. A future research phase should examine which financial questions people ask most often and which labels or chart conventions create uncertainty.
methods: Interface walkthrough
Examined the dashboard, transaction, wallet, and statistics destinations to understand the information available at each level.
Content review
Reviewed the sample target and cash-flow data in the source. Currency formatting, date conventions, and progress calculations need consistent rules before production use.
Task framing
Mapped orientation, inspection, comparison, and return navigation to identify where a summary needs supporting detail.

problem.statement: A financial dashboard can show many numbers without helping people understand how they relate. Goals, cash-flow trends, and transactions need a clear hierarchy and a dependable path to detail so a quick check can become an informed investigation.
problem.hmw: How might we connect financial summaries to the context people need, without overwhelming the overview?
constraints: Use demonstration data without implying real account connectivity.
Make time periods, currency conventions, and progress calculations understandable and consistent.
Support quick orientation and detailed review within the same navigation structure.

insights: Hierarchy should reflect the question
Goals, account context, and cash flow compete for attention. Their placement should help people distinguish current position from longer-term progress.
A chart needs a clear frame
A trend is useful only when its period and measure are understood. Labels and controls should explain what changes when a person switches the view.
Detail should explain the summary
Transactions and wallet views should preserve the context that prompted the visit. This connection is a key hypothesis for usability evaluation.
audiences: Everyday money manager
Needs a quick view of balances and recent activity, with a clear route to investigate an amount.
Goal-oriented planner
Needs to understand savings progress and compare activity across meaningful time periods.
journey: Group goals, activity, and account context.
A summary does not explain individual activity.
Account details can become detached from the overview.
Give wallet information a consistent workspace.
Charts can obscure the selected measure or period.
Keep period controls beside the report.
Detailed review can lose the bigger picture.
Preserve navigation back to the overview.

strategy.title: Support a quick check and a deeper look.
paragraphs: The dashboard establishes a starting point rather than attempting to contain every task. Savings targets, cash flow, and recent activity create a broad picture; dedicated destinations allow greater detail when a person needs it.

The strategy relies on consistent relationships between screens. A transaction amount should mean the same thing in the overview and the activity list, while a reporting period should remain explicit in statistical views. Clear content rules are therefore as important as the visual hierarchy.
priorities: Orientation through goals, cash flow, and recent activity.
Evaluate chart comprehension and reconcile sample-data conventions.

architecture.title: Organize the workspace around financial questions.
paragraphs: A persistent sidebar separates dashboard, transactions, wallet, and statistics. This creates stable destinations for overview, inspection, account context, and comparison. Supporting preferences remain separate from the main financial tasks.

The interface uses cards for bounded summaries, tables for comparable activity, and charts for change over time. Wireframe evaluation should focus on whether those choices help people answer a question rather than simply increase the amount of information on screen.
wireframes: Overview hierarchy
Compare the prominence of savings goals, cash flow, and account context during a short first impression.
Summary to detail
Test whether a person can find the transaction information needed to explain an overview amount.
Reporting controls
Check that a change of period or measure is understandable before refining the chart styling.

tradeoffs: Breadth versus focus
The overview covers several financial concerns. The hierarchy must make those groups readable without asking people to study every card.
Visual progress versus numerical precision
Progress rings aid scanning, but the displayed percentage and underlying amounts must agree. Reconcile sample data before evaluating trust in the interface.
Familiar patterns versus specific context
Cards and charts are familiar, but labels, periods, and formatting still need to explain this particular financial view.

paragraphs: The hosted dashboard and its transaction, wallet, and statistics navigation were inspected for this case study. These checks establish that the interface can be explored; they do not establish successful banking operations or user comprehension.

The proposed study should ask participants to explain the information in their own words and trace a summary to supporting detail. It should also test whether inconsistent sample formatting or progress values distract from the intended hierarchy.
tasks: Orient
Explain the dashboard’s goals, cash flow, and account context.
Distinguish current amounts from goals and period-based summaries.
Inspect activity
Find the transaction destination and identify an amount and category.
Locate relevant detail without losing the purpose of the investigation.
Compare periods
Explain the statistical report and its selected period.
Correctly describe what the chart represents.
Read goal progress
Compare a target amount, current amount, and percentage.
Recognize their relationship and flag any inconsistency.

paragraphs: The supplied frontend uses Next.js, TypeScript, and Tailwind, with reusable dashboard components and sample datasets. Product screenshots in this case study come from the hosted prototype, preserving the actual interface and its ArtoQu branding.

The next iteration should focus on consistent currency and date formatting, reconciled progress calculations, accessible chart alternatives, and clear empty and error states. Connecting live account data would require additional integration, security, and service-state design beyond the demonstrated frontend.
checks: Reconcile target percentages with current and target amounts.
Standardize currency separators, dates, and reporting periods.
Provide text alternatives for charts and keyboard access to controls.
Specify loading, empty, and error states before live integration.

executive.mandate: Create a welcoming home for faith-centered films, live programming, and audio, with a clear path from discovery to viewing.
executive.decision: Organize the experience around viewer intent and make access, content context, and return viewing explicit.
executive.value: Connect an independent product vision to a working web experience and a documented first-film rental milestone.

context: IreTV is my independent streaming-platform project. It brings Christian films, series, live television, children’s programming, podcasts, radio, and devotionals into one product. The central design challenge is to give that breadth a clear structure while helping a viewer make a confident choice about what to watch.

The product evolved from a movie-rental architecture into a broader viewing and listening experience. This case study follows that evolution using the project’s information architecture, design-system contract, saved interface iterations, current local screens, and first-film launch notes. The process board explains the design direction alongside product screens.
evidence: The saved UX specification defines Discover → Evaluate → Rent → Watch → Return and separates public discovery, rental, viewing, account, and administration.
Earlier captures show the movie-first prototype under the inherited Mighty Arrow design-system branding. Current local captures show the IreTV welcome and film pages.
The newer launch checklist records a controlled paid rental, a matching 14-day entitlement, and buyer-confirmed playback for The Travails of Maria. It also lists unresolved launch checks.

discovery.title: Start with the viewing decision, not the content grid.
paragraphs: The initial product specification provides a concrete discovery frame: a person needs to find something relevant, judge whether it fits the moment, understand the terms of access, watch successfully, and return later. That sequence makes the experience more than a collection of film posters. Each stage carries a different question, and the interface needs to answer it before asking for the next commitment.

The discovery approach separates the documented requirements from assumptions that still need viewer research. The requirements establish curated collections, content guidance, transparent rental terms, watchlists, and resume behavior. The working hypotheses concern why someone hesitates: uncertainty about suitability, confusion between free and paid content, or difficulty recovering a previous viewing session. These hypotheses guide the next evaluation rather than being presented as interview findings.
methods: Requirements synthesis
Map the existing product specification to the decisions a viewer makes before and after pressing play. Keep public discovery, account identity, and paid access separate.
Artifact review
Compare saved catalog, detail, and library iterations with the current product to explain how the hierarchy and brand evolved.
State and dependency mapping
Trace what happens when a viewer is signed out, has saved a film, has paid, has an expired rental, or cannot start playback.

problem.statement: A faith-centered catalog needs to communicate more than availability. Viewers need enough story and content context to choose confidently, a clear distinction between saving and accessing a title, and a dependable path back to their viewing. If those states blur together, a visually rich interface can still leave basic questions unanswered.
problem.hmw: How might we help viewers discover a meaningful title, understand their access, and continue watching with confidence?
constraints: Support multiple media formats without overloading the primary navigation.
Keep a saved title, a confirmed rental, and playback progress as distinct states.
Use the existing design system while allowing IreTV’s cinematic identity to develop.

insights: Suitability is part of discovery

The specification pairs synopsis and trailer with a Faith & Family Guide. The design hypothesis is that context about themes and content helps a household make its own choice; the platform should provide useful information rather than imply that one rating fits every family.
Saving is not ownership

A watchlist expresses interest. A rental grants time-limited access. Keeping those concepts separate avoids a misleading moment where a saved film appears playable or a completed payment is confused with a bookmark.
Return viewing needs its own architecture

Continue Watching, Watchlist, and History serve different intentions. Treating them as distinct library views helps a viewer resume unfinished content, revisit a saved choice, or find something previously watched.
audiences: Viewer choosing for a household
Needs story context, runtime, content guidance, and clear access terms before choosing a film. This is a provisional audience model, not a research persona.
Returning viewer or listener
Needs a familiar route back to saved content and previous progress across the product’s different media experiences.
journey: Find a relevant film or program
A broad catalog can feel undifferentiated
Use clear media categories and curated collections
Decide whether it fits the moment
Provide synopsis, trailer, runtime, and content guidance
Free, saved, and rented states can blur
Show the applicable access action and rental terms
A confirmed payment does not guarantee a working player
Connect entitlement checks, player feedback, and recovery
Resume or find a saved title
Progress and interest are different kinds of data
Separate Continue Watching, Watchlist, and History

strategy.title: Make one complete viewing journey work.
paragraphs: The early architecture is rental-first, while the current welcome experience introduces a wider mix of films, live programming, and audio. The strategic thread is the same: help someone move from intent to a useful viewing session. The first-film launch provides a concrete delivery slice inside that wider ambition, rather than requiring every platform feature to mature at once.

Scope also needs to reflect implementation reality. The project has account and library code, a first-film payment and entitlement flow, and documented playback checks. Broader household controls and some account surfaces remain previews in the older documentation. The case study therefore describes specific delivered capabilities and open work instead of implying the entire platform is complete.
priorities: Discovery hierarchy, film evaluation, account identity, and a persistent library.
The Travails of Maria: explicit offer, authenticated checkout, verified access, and protected playback.
Complete remaining launch checks, evaluate viewer comprehension, and refine cross-format navigation.

architecture.title: Separate where to look from what you can do.
paragraphs: The information architecture groups public discovery, title evaluation, access, playback, and the personal library. Within discovery, genres classify the catalog while collections provide an editorial lens such as a viewing occasion or theme. This distinction lets the product merchandise content without constantly changing its underlying classification.

The concept wireframes below reduces the experience to three decisions: find a title, evaluate it, and return to it. Its purpose is to expose hierarchy and state relationships beneath the final artwork. The complete product specification also covers checkout, payment failure, expiration, and playback recovery.
wireframes: Discover
Give the featured title one clear action, then offer curated groups and a visible route to search.
Evaluate
Place story context and access terms near the primary action; keep trailer and watchlist as distinct alternatives.
Return
Separate unfinished viewing from saved interest and history, with a clear status and next action for each title.

tradeoffs: Cinematic presentation versus decision clarity

Large artwork establishes the entertainment experience, but it cannot substitute for runtime, synopsis, content guidance, and access terms. The interface needs enough contrast and hierarchy for those details to remain readable over imagery.
Account continuity versus browsing friction

Accounts support private libraries and progress, but authentication can interrupt discovery. The current local welcome journey leads into sign-in for catalog exploration. That boundary deserves usability testing: a viewer should understand why an account is needed and retain the context that prompted the action.
Broad platform ambition versus a dependable launch

Films, live television, kids programming, and audio create a compelling vision but also different playback and persistence requirements. A complete, verified first-film path is a stronger delivery milestone than presenting every design preview as production-ready.

paragraphs: The available evidence includes technical and launch checks rather than a documented viewer usability study. The newer launch checklist records one controlled paid capture, a matching 336-hour entitlement, and buyer-confirmed playback. It also records an initial playback referrer issue that was fixed, plus checks denying playback to signed-out and unpaid requests. Those are useful delivery signals, but they do not establish general usability or conversion performance.

The next evaluation should observe how people interpret the experience. Use the tasks below with representative viewers, ask them to explain their understanding in their own words, and record hesitation as well as completion. No participant counts, satisfaction scores, or conversion improvements are invented here. Real refund behavior, territory coverage, account-email flows, and support readiness remain explicit follow-ups in the launch documentation.
tasks: Choose for a household
Find a film for an evening together and explain why it fits.
Locate relevant story, runtime, and content guidance without relying only on artwork.
Explain access
Compare a saved film, free content, and the featured rental before committing.
Distinguish saving from access and accurately describe the applicable price and viewing window.
Return and recover
Resume an interrupted title, then encounter an unavailable or expired state.
Find the correct library item, understand the status, and identify the appropriate next step.

paragraphs: The implementation uses a shared component and token system for navigation, cards, forms, dialogs, tabs, and feedback. The existing design-system contract explicitly favors adapting compositions over adding page-specific styling. That provides continuity across a cinematic public experience and more functional account and library screens.

For the first paid film, the important handoff boundary is between the customer’s payment action and confirmed access. The project implements server-side verification and time-limited playback access; a browser success message alone is not treated as permission to watch. From a UX perspective, the same distinction must remain visible in pending, failed, expired, and recovery states. Accessibility work should cover keyboard navigation through content rails, dialog focus, text over artwork, captions where available, and understandable playback feedback.
checks: Consistent access language across detail, checkout, library, and player.
Clear state handling for pending payment, failed playback, expiration, and return viewing.
Keyboard and focus behavior, readable imagery overlays, and accessible media controls.

executive.mandate: Make cross-border payments and digital asset management understandable within one account.
executive.decision: Organize the experience around customer intent, with destination, conversion and review made explicit.
executive.value: Help people understand where their money is, where it will go, and what they must check before committing.

context: Enta brings local bank rails and digital assets into the same product experience. Its public interface supports receiving, sending, buying and holding, with separate entry points for individuals and businesses. That breadth creates a design challenge: a familiar action such as sending money can involve different currencies, destinations and processing conditions.

As Lead Designer, my responsibility is represented here through the product experience and interface decisions. The case study examines the publicly visible dashboard and transaction demonstrations, focusing on hierarchy, decision clarity and continuity across steps. The screens show demonstration data rather than customer accounts.

discovery.title: Follow the money task, not the underlying technology.
paragraphs: The discovery frame begins with the customer’s situation: receiving income, paying someone, buying an asset, or checking a balance. Each situation calls for different information, even when it shares the same payment infrastructure. Mapping these intents helps distinguish the customer’s goal from the technical choices the system must resolve.

The public product walkthrough provides a concrete starting point for reviewing terminology, sequence and feedback. The key questions concern the moment a destination is selected, the point a conversion becomes clear, and the transition from an instruction to a confirmed transaction. These observations inform the design hypotheses below; they are not presented as interview findings.
methods: Task walkthrough
Trace the visible send, purchase and wallet flows. Identify what the customer needs to know before each consequential choice.
Information hierarchy review
Compare account-level totals with asset-level amounts, transaction activity and action controls. Check whether each answers a distinct question.
State and dependency mapping
Separate a quote, an order, payment instructions and confirmed receipt. Identify where external bank or network processing can interrupt the journey.

problem.statement: People moving between local currency and digital assets need to understand the destination, conversion and status of their money. When technical distinctions or processing steps are implicit, a simple task can become difficult to verify or recover.
problem.hmw: How might we make moving and holding money feel coherent while keeping the details of each transaction visible?
constraints: Keep currency, asset and network meanings distinct.
Show the amount paid and received before commitment.
Explain pending and time-sensitive steps without implying completion.

insights: Intent provides the entry point
Send, receive, buy and hold describe recognizable goals. Technical choices should appear when they are relevant to the selected goal, with enough context to support a correct decision.
A balance is only useful with context
A combined total supports orientation, but the individual holdings and display currency remain important. People need to understand what the number represents before moving money.
Instructions and confirmation are different states
A purchase can require a bank payment after an order is created. The interface needs to explain what remains to be done and preserve access to the transaction record.
audiences: Individual moving money across borders
Needs to understand destination, recipient amount and the next step without decoding infrastructure terminology.
Customer managing multiple holdings
Needs a coherent overview with enough asset-level detail to make an informed action.
journey: Different holdings can obscure what a total means
Show the display currency and asset breakdown
Paid and received amounts may be confused
Pair amounts, currency and relevant details
An order may still need external payment
Submitted may be mistaken for completed
Retain status and access to transaction detail

strategy.title: Build a coherent account around distinct money tasks.
paragraphs: The experience uses a shared account model while allowing each transaction type to expose its own requirements. A single generic form would conceal meaningful differences between a bank destination and an external wallet. Separate task entry points preserve those distinctions without fragmenting the overall experience.

The scope prioritizes orientation, destination selection and review. These are the points where interface clarity can support informed action. Additional services should inherit the same language for amounts, states and next steps so that breadth does not erode consistency.
priorities: Account orientation, clear task entry and destination-specific review.
Consistent transaction tracking and guidance when an external step remains.
Broader services using the same amount, status and confirmation patterns.

architecture.title: Move from account overview to a focused transaction.
paragraphs: The public dashboard places balances, recent transactions and transaction tools within a persistent account shell. Navigation separates wallets, payment links, beneficiaries and transactions. This lets a customer orient at account level before entering a task that requires more concentrated attention.

The transaction model progresses from intent to relevant details, review, required action and status. A low-fidelity exploration should test that hierarchy before visual polish: can someone distinguish the amount they send from what arrives, identify the selected destination, and explain whether another action is needed?
wireframes: Account overview
Prioritize the balance context and common actions; retain access to recent activity.
Transaction review
Bring destination, paid amount, received amount and relevant conditions into one decision surface.
Instructions and status
Separate the remaining action from the transaction record, with a clear path back to details.

tradeoffs: A unified account versus different payment routes
Shared navigation helps orientation, but transaction forms need to respect route-specific information. Consistency should preserve meaning rather than force every flow into identical fields.
A simple total versus financial detail
An aggregate balance is useful for scanning. Individual holdings and display currency should remain accessible so the summary does not obscure its components.
Motion versus readability
Animated demonstrations can explain sequence, but a case-study reader also needs stable frames to inspect labels and hierarchy. Still captures are paired with a link to the live demonstration.

paragraphs: The proposed evaluation should focus on comprehension before speed. Ask participants to describe the destination, amount paid, amount received and next required action at each key step. Observe misunderstandings without explaining the interface in advance.

Include incomplete and delayed scenarios alongside the happy path. A successful evaluation should show whether someone can distinguish an order from a completed payment and locate a useful transaction record. No participant counts or measured improvements are claimed here.
tasks: Choose a destination
Send to a bank account rather than an external wallet.
Customer chooses the appropriate route and explains the distinction.
Review a purchase
Explain what is paid and what is received before continuing.
Customer identifies both amounts and their currencies correctly.
Understand an incomplete order
Encounter bank payment instructions before completion.
Customer recognizes the outstanding action and finds the order details.

paragraphs: Delivery should translate the visual sequence into an explicit state model. The interface needs dependable labels for initiation, review, required payment, pending processing, completion and failure. Time-sensitive instructions should state what happens when their window expires and how the customer can safely continue.

Reusable amount displays, destination summaries and status messages can keep the experience consistent across transaction routes. Keyboard operation, clear focus, readable labels and reduced-motion behavior should accompany the visual design. The public product demos provide the visual reference for this case study; the live experience is linked for readers who want to see the interaction sequence.
checks: Currency, asset and destination labels across review surfaces
Distinct instructions, pending and confirmed states
Accessible controls, status announcements and reduced motion

executive.mandate: Give partner teams a shared view of collection, conversion and settlement.
executive.decision: Separate lifecycle stages and connect exceptions to the evidence needed to investigate them.
executive.value: Support clearer reconciliation and handoffs between operations, finance and integration teams.

context: Pulse is a settlement platform connecting digital assets and local currency. The partner experience sits between an integration and the people responsible for its operation. An API can initiate a flow, but a team still needs to understand which payments arrived, which converted, which settled, and which require attention.

This case study focuses on the partner console visible in Pulse’s public interactive demo. The dashboard, transaction list, exception detail and webhook screens provide a connected view of the operating model. Their figures and customer records are Test-mode examples; they illustrate interface behavior rather than measured business performance.

discovery.title: Find the gaps between a payment event and an operational answer.
paragraphs: The discovery frame follows one order across systems and responsibilities. A customer may have paid while conversion is pending, settlement has failed, or an amount mismatch requires review. Treating these situations as one generic processing state would obscure both the cause and the next responsible team.

Reviewing the public demo reveals the questions the experience must answer at different levels. The dashboard summarizes activity, the transaction list supports comparison, and the detail page provides a sequence of evidence. The proposed discovery work would test that hierarchy with operational and integration roles, particularly during exceptions.
methods: Lifecycle walkthrough
Follow an order from its pegged amount through payment, conversion and settlement. Record where each stage changes the meaning of the transaction.
Exception comparison
Compare underpaid, expired, failed and unsettled examples. Check whether labels distinguish what happened from what remains unresolved.
Cross-role information review
Identify the fields finance needs for reconciliation, the status operations needs for triage, and the event evidence developers need for diagnosis.

problem.statement: Partner teams need to explain and reconcile money movement across multiple stages. When incoming payment, conversion and settlement are collapsed into a single status, they cannot reliably identify a delay, understand an amount mismatch, or determine where investigation should begin.
problem.hmw: How might we make every payment’s progress and exceptions understandable across operations, finance and engineering?
constraints: Preserve the distinction between received, converted and settled value.
Keep amounts, currencies and transaction identifiers readable in dense views.
Expose exceptions without implying that every operator has authority to resolve them.

insights: A transaction has several meaningful amounts
Expected value, received payment and settled value answer different operational questions. Keeping them separate reduces ambiguity in both scanning and investigation.
Exceptions need an explanation, not just a badge
An underpayment label becomes useful when it is paired with the expected amount, actual amount and difference. The next layer should show which stages remain pending.
Integration delivery is part of operational visibility
A partner may need to know whether an event was delivered as well as whether a payment progressed. Transaction evidence and webhook monitoring serve related but distinct questions.
audiences: Finance and payment operations
Need to reconcile amounts, triage exceptions and explain the current state of a transaction.
Partner integration team
Needs to inspect event delivery and understand whether the integration is receiving lifecycle updates.
journey: Aggregate activity can conceal unresolved orders
Separate performance measures and attention queues
Dense records are difficult to scan
Use search, filters and explicit status labels
Expected and received values may be conflated
Display pegged, paid and settled amounts separately
Connect warnings, timeline and transaction details
Payment state and event delivery can diverge

strategy.title: Design the console around the questions teams need to answer.
paragraphs: The operating strategy connects summary, comparison and investigation. A dashboard should help someone decide where to look; a list should help them find the relevant record; a detail page should explain that record. Each level has a distinct purpose, so the interface can become more detailed without becoming repetitive.

The first priority is a coherent lifecycle vocabulary. Labels such as paid, converted and settled must carry the same meaning in cards, tables and timelines. Integration tools then extend the view to event delivery, without forcing every operator to work through developer terminology to understand a payment.
priorities: Settlement overview, transaction search and evidence-led exception detail.
Consistent event delivery visibility and clear handoffs between teams.
Broader reporting and configuration built on the same lifecycle definitions.

architecture.title: Create a path from business performance to transaction evidence.
paragraphs: The public console separates workspace functions from developer tools and organization settings. Home and Transactions support the frequent operational loop, while Webhooks and other integration controls remain available in a distinct navigation group. This preserves access without giving every function equal prominence.

Within a transaction, the exception summary precedes the timeline and supporting details. The low-fidelity question is whether that order matches the operator’s reasoning: what is wrong, how far did the transaction progress, and what evidence identifies it? The structure should support that sequence before adding more controls.
wireframes: Monitoring overview
Separate settled volume, activity and settlement rate; provide a route into unresolved work.
Comparison table
Keep customer, amount, asset and status aligned for scanning and investigation.
Exception workspace
Place the issue above a stage timeline, with identifiers and settlement details alongside.

tradeoffs: Information density versus scanability

Operations needs detailed records, but dense tables can make critical distinctions harder to see. Stable column alignment and explicit status text help preserve comparison while detail pages hold the deeper evidence.
Shared visibility versus role-specific control

Finance and developers benefit from a common transaction reference. That does not mean they need identical permissions or actions. The information architecture should support a shared understanding with appropriate control boundaries.
Summary metrics versus diagnostic evidence
A settlement rate can signal a question but cannot explain an individual exception. The dashboard should lead into supporting records rather than become a substitute for investigation.

paragraphs: The proposed evaluation would test whether participants can explain the lifecycle in their own words. Give an operator a paid but unsettled record and ask whether the partner has received the funds. Give a finance reviewer an underpayment and ask which values establish the discrepancy.

For integration work, test whether a developer can distinguish transaction progress from event delivery. Observe the path from a record to its supporting evidence and note any terminology that causes the participant to infer completion too early. These are proposed evaluation scenarios, not reported study results.
tasks: Reconcile a record
Compare the pegged, customer-paid and settled amounts.
Reviewer identifies the meaning and currency of each amount.
Investigate underpayment
Explain the warning and remaining timeline stages.
Operator identifies the mismatch without confusing it with completed settlement.
Check integration visibility
Inspect webhook delivery alongside transaction evidence.
Developer distinguishes event delivery from the underlying payment state.

paragraphs: Implementation should preserve the lifecycle model across data, labels and interaction states. The same order should not appear complete in one surface while retaining an unexplained pending state elsewhere. Empty, stale, failed and partially completed states need defined behavior alongside the populated Test-mode examples.

Reusable tables, status labels, amount formatting and timeline components can support consistency across the console. Accessible table headers, keyboard navigation, readable focus states and text equivalents for colored status indicators are particularly important in dense operational interfaces. The public demo is linked so readers can explore these screens in context.
checks: Consistent amount and status definitions across summary and detail
Role-aware actions and clear Test-mode context
Readable tables, keyboard access and non-color status meaning

executive.mandate: Make newsletter creation approachable through reusable pieces and practical starting points.
executive.decision: Combine templates, a searchable component palette, a live canvas and contextual editing in one workspace.
executive.value: Let authors spend more attention on their message while retaining control of structure and visual presentation.

context: Sendory is an innovation project exploring a familiar production problem: creating a newsletter requires content, layout, hierarchy and visual consistency to come together. Starting from an empty canvas makes every edition feel like a new design exercise, while a rigid template can become difficult to adapt when the message changes.

My work explores a middle ground: a composition system with reusable elements and flexible templates. The saved interactive prototype makes that idea tangible through a building-block palette, a central newsletter canvas and a properties inspector. The case study follows how those parts help an author start, assemble, refine and review an edition.
evidence: The saved app includes eight layout structures, 24 content blocks, three starter templates, undo/redo, local saving and preview controls.
Project QA notes record checks of block addition, nested layouts, contextual properties, insertion feedback and preview behavior.
The screens show the existing application with a sample newsletter composed for this walkthrough. They are product demonstrations rather than historical research records.

discovery.title: Understand the work hidden inside “make a newsletter.”
paragraphs: The starting point is the composition task described in the project: an author needs components, elements and templates readily available so they can turn content into a polished newsletter. That task involves several kinds of decisions. Choosing a structure is different from writing a headline, adjusting spacing or checking the result on a narrow screen.

The design exploration separates those decisions into a sequence: start with a purpose, assemble the message, adjust individual pieces, inspect the whole, and retain the work. Reviewing the saved implementation and its QA notes provides evidence of the intended interaction model. The audience needs below are design hypotheses; no interview counts or research quotations are assumed.
methods: Task decomposition
Map the steps between an idea and a reviewable edition. Identify where layout choices interrupt writing or where content changes require structural adjustment.
Component inventory
Separate layout primitives from content modules, then inspect which settings each type genuinely needs. Avoid presenting every control for every selection.
Prototype walkthrough
Exercise template loading, text editing, component search, layout selection and preview switching. Compare the authoring surface with the reader-facing presentation.

problem.statement: Newsletter authors need to combine varied content into a coherent, polished edition. A blank canvas demands too many initial design decisions, while inflexible templates make adaptation difficult. The experience needs to provide structure without removing useful creative control.
problem.hmw: How might we help people compose a distinctive newsletter from reusable pieces without asking them to design every detail from scratch?
constraints: Support both template-led and blank-canvas starting points.
Keep structural layout choices distinct from content editing.
Make changes reversible and the resulting presentation easy to inspect.

insights: Starting is a design decision
A useful template does more than supply decoration: it proposes a sequence of content. Naming templates by communication purpose helps authors choose a starting structure.
Reuse needs composability
A card, event or call to action becomes more useful when it can sit within different layouts. Separating the content module from its container makes reuse more flexible.
Polish comes from visible feedback
Authors need to see the effect of typography, color and spacing changes close to the controls that caused them. A separate preview provides a second perspective without editing boundaries.
audiences: Newsletter author
Needs a practical starting point, recognizable content blocks and a clear way to revise an edition.
Designer supporting recurring communication
Needs reusable patterns and enough control to guide hierarchy, spacing and presentation across varied content.
journey: An empty canvas creates too many initial choices
Authors must repeatedly recreate familiar sections
Provide searchable layout and content libraries
Show properties that match the selected block
Editing outlines obscure the final presentation
Offer clean desktop, tablet and mobile previews
Experiments can be lost or difficult to reverse

strategy.title: Make reuse the foundation of creative control.
paragraphs: The innovation is the relationship between the building blocks, rather than the number of controls. A template provides a beginning; layout primitives provide structure; content modules supply recurring communication patterns. Together they create a workspace in which a polished result can emerge from composition instead of repeated manual formatting.

The prototype prioritizes that authoring loop over campaign operations. Its strongest demonstrated capabilities are assembling, editing and previewing. Features such as production email delivery, collaboration and email-client rendering require their own implementation and verification; they should not be inferred from a button label in the prototype.
priorities: Template selection, reusable blocks, live composition and contextual properties.
Reliable reuse and recovery, with clear preview and persistence behavior.
Production delivery and email-client compatibility after the authoring model is validated.

architecture.title: Give each part of the workspace a clear responsibility.
paragraphs: The interface uses three working areas: discover blocks on the left, compose in the center, and refine the selection on the right. The top toolbar keeps document-level actions separate from block-level settings. This division helps the author understand whether an action changes the whole newsletter or only the selected element.

Layout and content are represented differently in the palette. A layout provides a place for children; a content block supplies a familiar unit such as a title, paragraph, card or event. The implementation also provides move, duplicate and delete actions on selections, while undo/redo supports experimentation across the composition.
wireframes: Palette and starting points
Group layout and content choices, with search and templates available before composing.
Live composition canvas
Make selection and insertion locations visible while keeping the newsletter hierarchy recognizable.
Contextual inspector
Separate canvas settings, layout controls and content properties according to the active selection.

tradeoffs: Guidance versus freedom

Starter templates reduce the decisions needed to begin, but the underlying blocks must remain editable. The composition should be a useful starting point rather than a fixed result the author has to work around.
Discoverability versus palette size
A broad block library supports varied content but increases scanning effort. Categories, recognizable names and search provide different ways to find the right component.
Editing affordances versus reader clarity
Borders, drop targets and action controls are useful while building. Removing them in Preview creates a cleaner review surface without hiding the tools during authoring.

paragraphs: A current walkthrough confirmed that a starter template loads into the canvas, text changes appear in the composition, palette search narrows the available blocks, and selecting a layout changes the inspector controls. Desktop and Mobile preview were opened for the same sample newsletter. Earlier project QA also records checks of undo/redo, nested insertion and clean preview rendering.

These are functional checks of the prototype. A usability study would ask authors to create a realistic edition, adapt its layout and review it without coaching. Observe where they confuse layout with content, cannot find a block, or lose confidence after a change. The study should establish whether the component model helps people compose—not assume a time-saving percentage in advance.
tasks: Start an edition
Choose a suitable template and replace its sample content.
Author recognizes the starting structure and can make it their own.
Adapt the composition
Find a content block and adjust a layout or property.
Author distinguishes structural controls from content editing.
Review and recover
Inspect a narrow preview and undo an unwanted change.
Author can identify presentation issues and return to a useful state.

paragraphs: The saved prototype is a working exploration of the authoring experience, with local persistence and a basic HTML export path. Its export implementation does not establish faithful output for every complex or nested component, and an in-browser preview does not establish compatibility with email clients. Those boundaries shape the handoff requirements.

A production implementation should define a portable document model, component serialization, supported email markup and a rendering test matrix. Accessibility should cover keyboard insertion and reordering as well as pointer interactions. Shared spacing and typography rules can preserve consistency while leaving room for each newsletter’s content and identity.
checks: Document structure and component serialization, including nested layouts
Undo, persistence and recovery for authoring changes
Keyboard composition and focus behavior
Email-client rendering and delivery verification before production sending

executive.mandate: Explore how people can compose AI-assisted workflows while retaining visibility into the steps, decisions, and operational consequences.
executive.decision: Make the proposed plan reviewable, the workflow editable, and the human handoff visible before introducing execution complexity.
executive.value: The prototype demonstrates a connected authoring and oversight experience. Its value proposition is clearer control of automation; adoption and efficiency gains remain to be evaluated.

context: Flownode explores the gap between describing an automation and trusting it enough to use it. A natural-language request can express an intention quickly, but the resulting workflow still needs a structure that people can understand, revise, and supervise. The design connects that initial request to an inspectable plan and a graphical workflow.

The supplied React and TypeScript application provides the basis for this case study. Its canvas, configuration panels, plan builder, execution history, and operations screens form an interactive frontend prototype. Authentication, generated plans, and execution activity are simulated; the screens demonstrate the experience rather than a deployed automation service.

discovery.title: Examine where intention becomes uncertainty.
paragraphs: The starting point is the workflow represented in the prototype: choose or describe an automation, review its steps, configure the graph, and inspect activity. Examining this sequence surfaces several design questions. Can someone explain what a generated plan will do? Can they identify the step that requires their judgment? Can they distinguish a waiting task from a failed one?

These questions frame a product opportunity without implying completed user interviews. The discovery work presented here is an examination of the supplied interface and implementation, with audience needs expressed as hypotheses for future research.
methods: Interface walkthrough
Reviewed the dashboard, AI plan modal, canvas, configuration panel, execution history, and operations view to connect the authoring experience with its oversight surfaces.
Implementation review
Examined seeded workflow data and the local plan-selection logic. This identifies which behaviors are interactive and which depend on simulated responses.
Risk-oriented framing
Prioritized ambiguity around scope, human approval, execution status, and cost because each could affect whether a person understands the consequences of an automation.

problem.statement: People need a way to turn an automation intention into a workflow they can explain and control. A generated answer alone does not reveal enough about sequence, conditions, human responsibility, or the state of work after it starts.
problem.hmw: How might we make AI-assisted workflow creation feel inspectable at every consequential decision?
constraints: The available implementation is a frontend prototype with predefined plans and demonstration activity.
Complex graphs must remain understandable alongside detailed step settings.
Approval, errors, and cost need clear meaning before a live execution service can be connected.

insights: A proposal needs a review boundary
Separating plan generation from insertion gives people a moment to evaluate intent and scope. This is a design hypothesis about comprehension, not a measured finding.
Control needs a visible location
Putting approval into the graph makes the handoff tangible. The next question is whether people can recognize who acts and what remains paused.
Monitoring completes the authoring story
A workflow becomes an ongoing responsibility once it runs. Status and operational views should help explain what happened and what action is available.
audiences: Workflow author
Needs to translate an intended process into understandable steps and adjust the details without losing the overall sequence.
Operations reviewer
Needs to identify waiting or failed work, understand its context, and decide where human intervention is required.
journey: A short prompt can conceal important conditions.
Start from an example and make the proposed sequence explicit.
Check that the plan matches the intention.
Generated steps may imply actions the author did not expect.
Show the plan and estimated cost before insertion.
Adjust the workflow and its decisions.
Detailed settings can obscure the wider process.
Keep the canvas beside step configuration.
Waiting and failed states require different responses.
Use distinct statuses and an explicit human gate.
Individual runs do not reveal recurring problems.
Provide an operations view for failure and routing patterns.

strategy.title: Make the automation legible before making it powerful.
paragraphs: The experience is organized around progressive commitment. A person first expresses an intention, then reviews a proposed plan, and finally edits the workflow in context. Each stage introduces more detail while preserving an opportunity to revise the previous decision.

The Build and Operate navigation groups reflect two different modes of work. Authoring benefits from a focused canvas and configuration tools; oversight benefits from comparable statuses, activity records, and operational signals. The structure keeps these responsibilities connected without forcing them into one crowded screen.
priorities: Make each proposed step and its place in the sequence understandable.
Expose the points where configuration or human judgment changes what happens next.
Carry the workflow context into activity and operations views.

architecture.title: Connect the plan, the graph, and the operational record.
paragraphs: The prototype uses a persistent sidebar to establish the product’s major workspaces. The workflow canvas occupies the main authoring area, with step details available in an adjacent panel. This supports moving between the overall process and a specific setting without changing the underlying task context.

The AI plan modal acts as a transition between language and structure. Execution history then presents activity as a list, while operations aggregates signals across runs. Together, these surfaces demonstrate an information architecture that moves from intent to configuration to oversight.
wireframes: Plan hierarchy
Evaluate whether people notice the proposed sequence, approval requirement, and cost before accepting a plan.
Canvas and detail balance
Explore how much space the configuration panel can occupy before connections become difficult to follow.
Attention hierarchy
